lines.text:
Sending a Parcel

Yesterday, I went to the post office to send a birthday present to my cousin in another city. It was my first time sending a parcel, so I was not sure what to do.

When I arrived, there was a short queue at the counter. While I waited, I looked around. There were shelves with padded envelopes, cardboard boxes, packing tape, and bubble wrap. I picked up a medium-sized box and some tape.

At the counter, the postal worker weighed my parcel on a scale. It was just under two kilograms. She asked if I wanted to send it by standard delivery or express delivery. Standard takes three to five working days; express arrives the next day but costs more. I chose standard.

She gave me a form to fill in with the sender's address and the recipient's address. I also wrote the postcode carefully because, she explained, an incorrect postcode can delay the delivery.

I paid the postage fee and she stuck stamps and a tracking label on the box. She gave me a receipt with a tracking number so I could follow the parcel online.

Before I left, I also bought a book of stamps for regular letters and posted two letters in the postbox outside. The red pillar box had two slots: one for local mail and one for everything else.

Sending a parcel was easier than I expected. My cousin received it two days later and called to say thank you.

lines.text: UK post is handled by Royal Mail (red vans, red postboxes). US post is handled by USPS (blue mailboxes). Both have first-class (fast) and second-class/standard (slower, cheaper) options.

lines.text: The UK's iconic red pillar boxes have been used since 1852. They have the royal cipher of the reigning monarch at the time they were made. Some very old ones still have Queen Victoria's initials!

lines.text: 'Signed for' delivery requires someone to sign when the parcel arrives. 'Tracked' delivery shows the parcel's journey online. These options cost extra but provide proof of delivery.
